s: The team evaluated MongoDB and PostgreSQL for a product catalog with variable attributes, choosing MongoDB for its schema flexibility.
MongoDB chosen via Mongoose ODM with schemas for User, Product, and Order collections using embedded documents for order items.
MongoDB's document model provides schema flexibility for variable product attributes and embedded order items for single-fetch reads.
Lack of default ACID transactions complicates multi-document operations like order+inventory updates, and schema changes require manual migration scripts.
PostgreSQL with Sequelize/Prisma would have provided ACID compliance, mature query planner, and JOIN support, but was passed over for MongoDB's flexibility.
For the actual workload with fixed product schemas and modest traffic, PostgreSQL would have been an equally valid or better choice than MongoDB.
The frontend needed state management across cart, auth, server data cache, and UI dimensions, with Redux chosen over Context and newer alternatives.
Redux with redux-thunk was adopted with per-slice architecture: constants, actions, and reducers for cart, user, product, and order domains.
Migration to Redux Toolkit replaces hand-written constants/actions/reducers with createSlice and createAsyncThunk for reduced boilerplate.
Redux provides DevTools time-travel debugging and predictable state, at the cost of significant boilerplate from the REQUEST/SUCCESS/FAIL triple pattern.
Alternatives include React Context (poor re-render performance), React Query (server state only), Zustand (minimal), and RTK Query (planned migration).
Redux Toolkit remains the state management solution; RTK Query migration is planned for server data portions while RTK handles client state.
The Express API needed an authentication mechanism for browser and potential mobile clients, with no shared session store infrastructure.
JWT tokens signed with JWT_SECRET store user ID and isAdmin claim, stored in localStorage and sent as Bearer token in Authorization headers.
JWT provides stateless auth simplifying deployment, but introduces XSS risk via localStorage and inability to revoke tokens before 30-day expiry.
Alternatives include server-side sessions with MongoDB store, Passport.js, and OAuth-only login, each with trade-offs in complexity and revocation.
Open issues include implementing short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens via HttpOnly cookies to address revocation and XSS limitations.
JWT works for current use case; known limitations are accepted technical debt requiring addressing for higher-security contexts like payment processing.
The application needed a payment processor with sandbox testing, minimal PCI scope, and reasonable integration complexity for a two-person team.
PayPal integration via @paypal/react-paypal-js handles payment in a popup with onApprove callback sending PayPal order ID to backend for verification.
PayPal reduces PCI scope to SAQ A by handling card entry in its iframe, provides brand recognition, and supports multiple currencies.
PayPal sandbox fires onApprove twice under certain network conditions, requiring idempotency keys; limited UI customization is also a drawback.
Stripe was evaluated as the preferred alternative with faithful test mode, superior API design, and Stripe Elements for card input.
A mock-only payment approach was rejected because the goal was a realistic e-commerce application with functional payment flow.
Migration to Stripe would require Payment Intents, replacing PayPalButtons with Stripe Elements, and adding webhook handling.
PayPal integration is stable in production since v2.1 with no idempotency recurrence, but Stripe would be chosen for any new project.
The frontend needed a CSS framework for responsive layout and component primitives, with Bootstrap 4 chosen based on familiarity.
Bootstrap 4 adopted via react-bootstrap using the grid system, standard components, and a vendored pre-compiled CSS file.
Migration to Tailwind CSS deferred to v3.0 as a bundled effort with Vite migration, scoped at 5 engineer-days.
Bootstrap enabled rapid initial development but ships unused CSS styles and creates global specificity conflicts with custom overrides.
Tailwind CSS offers utility-first classes with tree-shaking via PurgeCSS for minimal bundles and no global CSS conflicts.
Material UI rejected for unwanted Material Design aesthetic; Chakra UI considered but adds dependency weight for a legacy project.
Migration plan: add Tailwind/PostCSS to Vite, remove react-bootstrap, rewrite components from layout to complex interactive elements.
Bootstrap 4 continues to function but the ecosystem gap grows with each deferral, making the eventual migration structurally harder.
The authentication API uses JWT tokens sent as Bearer tokens in the Authorization header with 30-day expiry.
Login endpoint authenticates via email/password returning JWT; registration creates account and returns JWT immediately.
Profile endpoints allow authenticated users to retrieve and update their own profile information via JWT Bearer token.
JWT flow: user authenticates, server signs token, client stores in localStorage, sends as Bearer header, server validates via protect middleware.
All auth API errors return JSON with a message field, using standard HTTP status codes: 400 for validation, 401 for auth failure.
Order endpoints manage the complete lifecycle: creation, retrieval, payment, and delivery tracking with role-based access.
Create order endpoint accepts cart items, shipping address, and payment method, calculating prices with default unpaid status.
Retrieves all orders for the authenticated user, sorted by date, requiring JWT Bearer token.
Retrieves detailed order information by ID including items, shipping, payment result, and delivery status.
Payment endpoint marks order as paid with PayPal details; delivery endpoint allows admin to mark as delivered.
Admin-only endpoint retrieves all orders in the system with full details, requiring admin JWT Bearer token.
Order data model includes user reference, order items array, shipping address, payment result, delivery status, and price fields.
Order lifecycle: create unpaid, PayPal payment, mark paid, admin delivery, mark delivered, with timestamps at each transition.
Standard HTTP response codes: 200 success, 201 created, 400 invalid input, 401 auth failure, 404 not found.
Product endpoints provide catalog listing with search/pagination, detail retrieval, admin CRUD, and user review submission.
Public product listing with keyword search and pagination; top-rated endpoint returns highest-rated products for carousel.
Product detail retrieval by ID is public; product creation is admin-only with sample template generation.
Admin-only endpoints for updating product details and deleting products by MongoDB ObjectId.
Authenticated users submit one review per product with 1-5 star rating and comment; duplicates and empty fields are rejected.
Product data model with name, price, description, image, brand, category, stock count, and embedded reviews with computed rating.
Standard response codes including 400 for duplicate reviews and 401 for unauthorized admin operations.
Upload endpoint handles product image uploads restricted to JPG/PNG format, 2MB max size, admin-only access.
POST /api/uploads accepts multipart form data with image field, validates format and size, returns file path.
Upload validation restricts to JPG/JPEG/PNG, enforces 2MB limit, validates both file extension and MIME type.
Upload flow: admin authenticates, POST with image, Multer validates extension/MIME/size, file saved with timestamp filename.
Files stored in uploads/ directory with timestamp-based filenames, served as static files by Express.
Usage examples for file upload using cURL, JavaScript Fetch API, and Axios with Authorization header.
Security measures for uploads: double validation (extension + MIME), 2MB size limit, admin authentication required.
Integration workflow: admin creates product with sample image, uploads actual image, updates product with new image path.
Common upload error scenarios: missing token (401), invalid/expired token (401), not admin (401), wrong file type (400).
Upload response codes: 200 for successful upload, 400 for validation errors, 401 for auth failure.
Server upload configuration: environment variables for upload directory, middleware stack with protect+admin, Express static serving.
User management endpoints are restricted to administrators for viewing, modifying, and deleting user accounts.
Admin-only endpoints for listing all users and retrieving individual user details by MongoDB ObjectId.
Admin endpoints for updating user account details (name, email, admin status) and deleting users.
All user management endpoints require valid JWT token plus isAdmin flag, enforced by protect + admin middleware chain.
User data model with fields for name, email, bcrypt-hashed password, and isAdmin boolean flag.
Standard response codes: 200 success, 400 validation error, 401 auth failure, 404 user not found.
ProShop is a full-stack MERN e-commerce application with product catalog, cart, checkout, PayPal payments, and admin panel.
Technology stack: Node.js runtime, Express 4 server, Mongoose 5 ODM, React 16 SPA with Redux 4, CRA with webpack 4.
Three-layer architecture: Browser (React SPA + Redux), Express API server, MongoDB database, with Axios as HTTP bridge.
Frontend bootstrapping: index.js wraps App in Redux Provider, store.js uses combineReducers with 20+ slices and redux-thunk middleware.
Redux store structure with 20+ combined slices covering products, cart, user auth, orders, and admin operations.
Action creators organized in four files following REQUEST/SUCCESS/FAIL triple pattern with Axios for API calls and JWT auth headers.
14 page-level screen components with Redux interaction, 7 reusable UI components, React Router 5 routing in App.js without lazy loading.
Checkout state lifecycle flows from cart through shipping, payment, and order creation with localStorage persistence at each step.
